questions.title: Ciprofloxacin's mechanism of action in acute bacterial prostatitis
questions.question: A 65-year-old man is diagnosed with acute bacterial prostatitis and is prescribed ciprofloxacin for 6 weeks. His agent acts by which of the following mechanisms?

options.B: Inhibition of bacterial cell wall synthesis

explanations.A: Incorrect. Competitive inhibition of para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) in the folate-synthesis pathway is the mechanism of the sulfonamides, not a fluoroquinolone; ciprofloxacin does not touch folate metabolism.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Inhibition of bacterial cell wall synthesis describes the beta-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins) and glycopeptides such as vancomycin, which act on peptidoglycan cross-linking, not on DNA replication.
explanations.C: Correct. Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone: it inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and, in Gram-positive organisms, topoisomerase IV, both of which are required to relieve supercoiling ahead of the replication fork. Blocking this step halts DNA replication and is bactericidal — the mechanism that makes fluoroquinolones effective for a deep-tissue infection like bacterial prostatitis, where good tissue penetration and a bactericidal action are both needed.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Reversible binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit describes macrolides (e.g., erythromycin) and clindamycin, which block protein synthesis — a different target and a different (usually bacteriostatic) class of action from ciprofloxacin's.

questions.learning_objective: State ciprofloxacin's mechanism of action and distinguish it from the other major antibacterial mechanism classes.
